planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow in a container that can be moved under cover for winter outside zones 9-11.

directions: This single-flowered Arabian jasmine cultivar is the classic form used for jasmine tea and Hawaiian lei-making, bearing clusters of small, round, intensely fragrant white blooms that open in waves from spring through fall. It stays more compact and mounding than the double-flowered 'Grand Duke of Tuscany', making it well suited to patio containers, low hedges, or a sheltered courtyard bed where its scent can be enjoyed up close. Give it warm, humid conditions with consistent moisture and monthly feeding during active growth, and pinch stem tips to encourage the branching habit that produces the heaviest bloom. Bring potted specimens indoors to a bright window well before the first frost, since foliage and stems are damaged below the mid-30s F.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or maintain as a container plant trained on a small trellis.

directions: This Arabian jasmine selection is distinguished by narrow, elongated white petals that give each semi-double bloom a distinctive spidery, star-like shape rather than the rounded form typical of the species. It has a looser, more vining habit than 'Maid of Orleans' and benefits from light staking or a small trellis to display its clustered, richly scented flowers, which open nearly year-round in frost-free conditions. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil with regular water and periodic light feeding, and shelter it from drying wind, which can scorch the thin petals. Where winters bring frost, keep it in a container and move it to a bright, humid indoor spot until temperatures warm again in spring.

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost against a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; growth is vigorous, so site it where regular pruning is feasible.

directions: This fast-growing, twining tropical vine produces clusters of pink-tinged buds that open to fragrant white, pinwheel-shaped flowers over an extended bloom season in warm climates. Its glossy, leathery leaves and vigorous, scrambling stems quickly cover an arbor, fence, or trellis, but it also roots readily where trailing stems touch soil, so prune regularly to keep growth contained and prevent it from naturalizing into surrounding beds. Provide fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil and feed lightly during the growing season to sustain steady flowering. In the northern part of its range it dies back to the ground after light frost but typically resprouts from the roots when grown in sheltered, warm-winter sites.

planting.note: Plant transplants in spring against a trellis, pergola, or wall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; in cooler zones grow it in a large container that can be sheltered over winter.

directions: This twining evergreen vine bears glossy, three-lobed leaflets and clusters of small, waxy white flowers that open from pink-tinged buds and carry a sweet fragrance reminiscent of common jasmine, most heavily through summer and into fall. It climbs by twining rather than clinging, so tie young growth to a trellis, arbor, or wires to establish a framework before it fills in. Grow it in fertile, well-drained soil with regular water during the growing season, and reduce watering somewhat in winter when growth slows. Where temperatures dip toward the mid-20s F, plant it in a protected microclimate or maintain it as a container specimen that can be moved to shelter.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it can be grown as a loose freestanding shrub or trained flat against a warm wall.

directions: This mounding to semi-scrambling evergreen or semi-evergreen shrub bears clusters of bright yellow flowers with a light, sweet fragrance, blooming most heavily in late spring and again intermittently through summer. Its glossy, compound leaves and naturally rounded habit make it useful as an informal flowering hedge or background shrub, and it also tolerates being trained against a warm, sheltered wall where reflected heat encourages more prolific bloom. Plant in average, well-drained soil and water regularly during establishment, tapering off once roots are established, since it tolerates brief dry spells once mature. Prune after the main spring flush to control size and shape, and protect the root zone with mulch in the colder part of its hardiness range.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
